Multivitamin Compliance Reduces Injuries of Female Recruits at Air Force Basic Training: A Randomized Controlled Cohort Study
Korey B. Kasper, MD, CAQSM *; Meredith Cockerell, MS,  ATC†; Clarissa Escamilla, MS, RDN, LD‡;
Richard Gonzalez, MDS, RDN, LD‡
ABSTRACT
Introduction:
Department of the Air Force basic military training (BMT) is the 7.5-week initial entry training for all enlisting U.S. Air Force and Space Force recruits. Overuse musculoskeletal injuries (MSKI) during training threaten success in BMT, and trainees with nutritional deficiencies are at higher risk. Several efforts are made at BMT to mitigate these issues to help trainees graduate on time, such as the distribution of multivitamins (MVI) to female recruits. However, trainee compliance with the prescribed MVI has been reported to be low, calling into question the effectiveness of this intervention. This study evaluated the effect of briefing modality offered to these trainees at the time of distribution on educational effectiveness, MVI compliance, and injury rates.
Materials and Methods:
This was a randomized controlled cohort study of BMT female trainees. Subjects included all female trainees of a single iteration of BMT concurrently completing training within the same squadron. At the outset of training, cohorts were randomly educated in one of two ways regarding the provided MVI. The control cohort ( n = 80) was presented with the standard educational video created by BMT-registered dietitians, while the test cohort ( n = 79) was presented the video and then also briefed in-person by a group of subject matter experts. At the end of BMT, the trainees completed a questionnaire regarding their knowledge, confidence, and compliance with the MVI. Additionally, a routinely collected training database was queried and analyzed for differences in injuries and training outcomes using the chi-squared test with significance set to α≤ 0.05.

Deficiencies occurring before BMT (baseline nutrition) and during BMT (relative to training demands or in response to exercise and adaptations) can interfere with training success via effects on musculoskeletal injury (MSKI), 6 illness, 7-9 and poor mental and physical adaptation and performance. 4,10-19\\nBone stress injury (BSI) is a specific overuse MSKI very common  in  military  recruits,  to  which  those  harboring  a nutritional deficiency are at higher risk. 20-23 In a recent publication, 13.87% of male trainees and 14.13% of female trainees were clinically diagnosed with BSI at BMT. 24 These conditions  result  in  increased  health  care  costs,  training  disruptions, delayed graduation ($384.33/day/trainee), and incompletion of training rates ( \\u223c $55 K/trainee attrition). 25 BSI and\\n* 559th Trainee Health Squadron, JBSA-Lackland, TX 78236, USA\\n\\u2020 59th  Medical  Wing,  Science  and  Technology,  JBSA-Lackland,  TX 78236, USA\\n\\u2021 37th Training Wing, Human Performance Directorate, JBSA-Lackland, TX 78236, USA\\nPresented  as  a  poster  at  the  2023  Military  Health  System  Research Symposium, Kissimmee, FL, United States; MHSRS-23-08081 'In-Person Female  Performance  Multivitamin  Briefing  Improves  Compliance  and Reduces Injuries at USAF Basic Military Training' presented as 'In-Person Briefing of Female Multivitamin Improves Compliance & Reduces Injuries at Air Force Basic Military Training' on August 15, 2023.\\nThe views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the official views or policy of the DoD or its components. For  permissions, please  e-mail: journals.permissions@oup.com.\\n\\n--- Page 2 ---\\nits nutritional risk factors (such as low-energy availability, 26 iron, 5,22,27 and calcium/vitamin D 28,29 )  thus  present important targets for prevention and mitigation efforts in military training.\\nBSI-facilitating nutritional deficits in BMT trainees occur for  myriad  reasons  which  have  been  reported  clinically  by trainees  to  the  clinicians  of  this  authorship  team.  Before BMT, trainees may be affected by food insecurity, knowledge deficits, and restricted diets. During BMT, intake of adequate nutrition  may be hindered by unavailability of preferred or religious food choices at the dining facilities (DFAC), lack of adequate mealtime in the DFAC, and appetite reductions associated with the stress of training. Regardless of the reasons, trainees with intentional or unintentional nutritional deficits at BMT are predisposed to worse training adaptation, which may lead to hindered performance as well as MSKI; such trainees are at higher risk to not graduate BMT on time or at all. 30\\nFor  these  reasons, BMT  has  taken  steps  to  improve the  fueling  of  trainees.  DFAC  food  product  offerings  have improved to  better  meet  nutritional  needs  and  specific  diet requirements of individuals.  Furthermore,  in BMT DFACs, changes to choice architecture and the introduction of the Go For Green\\u00ae program, 31 which provides quick assessments of menu item nutritional value,  have  helped  direct  trainees  to healthier choices. Beyond their three daily meals in the DFAC, since 2012, trainees have been provided an evening snack in the form of their choice of a fruit or nutrition bar 'to improve nutritional adequacy and timing in relation to exercise and as well as reduce attrition.' 4\\nFemale military trainees are at higher risk of nutritional deficiency,  most  notably  iron  deficiency, 5,32-34 injury, 23,30 and  attrition 35 compared  to  their  male  counterparts. To address  these  disproportionate  risks  and  'improve  performance and decrease rates of attrition,' a daily prenatal multivitamin (MVI) with iron has been prescribed and distributed to females arriving to BMT, since 2012. 35 Of note, this MVI is labeled 'prenatal' because of its folic acid content (which is  recommended  for  all  females  of  child-bearing  potential per  the  Centers  for  Disease  Control  and  Prevention 36 and the United States Preventive Services Task Force 37 ) and was chosen because prenatal MVIs are on the organization's formulary whereas other MVIs are not. However, the MVI was chosen specifically for vitamin D and iron supplementation. The contents of this MVI are listed in Table I. Though the vitamin D content (400 IU) is half the dose associated with decreased  stress  fractures  among  navy  recruits  reported  by Lappe et al., 28 the 27 mg of iron approximates the estimated 22 mg daily requirement for females in military training. 8\\nA study by Barnes et al. 35 retrospectively investigated the effects of prescribing this MVI to female trainees and 'found a  statistically  nonsignificant  effect  of  prenatal  vitamin  supplementation on attrition from training and on development of stress fractures and iron deficiency anemia among females undergoing U.S. Air Force BMT' but deemed the 26% associated reduction in medical attrition as 'operationally adequate to justify continuation' of the program. Those authors noted limitations from its nonrandomized, retrospective nature comparing trainees who were prescribed the prenatal and counseled  on  its  potential  benefits  and  risks  with  a  historical season-matched  control  group  that  previously  matriculated BMT and lack of assessment of compliance. A 2014 survey of female BMT trainees found that less than half reported daily MVI compliance. 35\\nTABLE I. Supplement Facts of the Prenatal MVI Distributed to Females at BMT\\nDespite the statistically nonsignificant findings, MVI prescriptions  for  female  trainees  have  continued  at  BMT  with briefings given in various forms. The process of education and distribution of this MVI occurs during medical in-processing, during the first week of BMT; since 2020, groups of female trainees have been shown a video put together by embedded registered  dietitians  (RD).  In  the  video,  BMT  RDs  review the purpose of the MVI, its contents, potential benefits, and how  and  when  to  take  it.  Trainees  may  ask  questions  of an  enlisted  medical  technician  before  the  distribution  of  a 3-month  supply  of  the  MVI.  However,  anecdotally,  many trainees  reported  poor  compliance  with  the  MVI,  either  by choice or forgetfulness.\\nCountless  questions  remain  regarding  the  effectiveness and efficacy of dietary supplementation for injury and performance  improvements, and  specifically  within  military trainees for improved operational outcomes. Despite the effort and resources appropriated for providing an MVI with iron to all female trainees, the intended benefits have not conclusively been demonstrated. 35 Issues with compliance as well as nutrient timing and dosage in relation to the high stresses of BMT may preclude realization of performance, injury, and attrition benefits. This study aimed to determine whether the addition of  an  in-person  brief  of  the  MVI  by  subject-matter  experts (SMEs)  at  the  time  of  distribution  would  improve  female BMT trainee knowledge, confidence, and compliance with the MVI and whether this, in turn, would affect MSKI/BSI incidence and training outcomes.  On the other hand,  improved compliance without a corresponding improvement of injury incidence or training outcomes could encourage BMT trainee health leadership to support discontinuation the MVI process at BMT for cost and time savings.\\n\\n--- Page 3 ---\\nMETHODS\\nEvery recruit arriving to BMT in the same week is assigned to the same 'squadron' for housing and training and are further divided into 'flights' (groups of \\u223c 40 trainees of the same gender). Female trainees medically in-process as a unit with their flight  mates,  during which time they receive the MVI. The start date for a recruit is essentially random as is the flight to which they are assigned by BMT leadership.\\nAll female trainees from a single training squadron who concurrently entered BMT in December 2021, and who had already been randomly assigned to 1 of the 4 flights,  were enrolled in this command-directed process improvement evaluation.  These  flights  were  randomly  assigned  to  cohorts, which  would  receive  one  of  two  MVI-briefing  modalities. The control cohort consisted of every recruit within 2 female trainee flights, which received standard MVI education via the BMT RD video with medical technician facilitation ('videoonly'  cohort).  The  test  cohort  consisted  of  every  recruit within  the  other  2  female  trainee  flights,  which  were  presented  the  same  video  and  reviewed  important  information with  an  in-person  team  of  SMEs  (the  trainee  health  clinic medical  director/sports  medicine  physician,  RD,  and  diet technician) and were given an opportunity to ask questions ('in-person' cohort). Because this study was designed as an internal,  commander-directed  process  improvement  evaluation, and obtaining individual consent from each member of the squadron was deemed overly burdensome and costly to the training and medical processing schedule, trainees were not made aware that their briefing experience was different from that of any others; this was further deemed crucial since trainee knowledge of their compliance being assessed would likely skew their compliance and report thereof.  Flight and squadron leadership were also not made aware of the change in  education,  nor  were  other  medical  providers.  No  other cohort differences with regards to MVI distribution,  education,  training,  or  medical  care  occurred  for  the  entirety  of BMT. After  the  completion  of  BMT,  injury,  performance, and  outcome  data  (regularly  tracked  for  all  BMT  trainees)\\nTABLE II. Demographic Characteristics of Participants\\nValues are reported as averages \\u00b1 standard deviations (SD). BMI calculated using height (meters) and weight (kilograms).\\nwere  compiled  for  these  female  flights;  this  and  the  survey  results  were  then  compared  between  the  flights  that received  the  video-only  or  the  in-person  MVI  education. There  was  no  crossing  over  between  flights/cohorts.  The Institutional  Review  Board  at  the  59th  Medical  Wing  at JBSA-Lackland approved the project as an exempt protocol (FWH20220101E).\\nMultiple  routinely  collected  and  manually  linked  (person  level,  via  full  name  and  DoD  identification  number) databases were queried for this study. The Electronic Basic Training Management System is maintained by Air Education and Training Command and stores demographic data such as squadron and flight assignment, age, gender (as identified in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System), body mass index (BMI), and training outcome data (e.g., attrition and training delays). A database of MSKI diagnosed at BMT is  maintained  by  sports  medicine  staff,  which  is  routinely analyzed by members of the study team for injury trend monitoring and program improvement. Furthermore, all trainees completed questionnaires regarding their perceptions regarding the usefulness and effectiveness of their MVI briefing and were asked to quantify their MVI compliance. All data linkage and analysis (injury, training delays, graduation, briefing perceptions, and compliance) occurred following completion of the training period.\\nFor this prospective, randomized controlled cohort study, a power analysis calculation was completed using \\u03b1\\u2264 0.05 for the significance level, a power of 0.99. We estimated a 25% relatively greater daily MVI compliance in trainees receiving the in-person brief compared to those viewing the video alone, which yielded a need for each cohort to have 77 trainees to demonstrate a significant difference.\\nAssociations between categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-squared test. Significance was set to \\u03b1\\u2264 0.05. Statistical  analyses  were  performed  using  SAS  version  9.4 (Statistical Analysis Software, Cary, NC).\\nRESULTS\\nDemographic characteristics of the 159 female trainees (80 in the video-only cohort,  and 79 in the in-person cohort) subjected to this study are provided in Table II. No significant differences in age or BMI between cohorts were detected.\\nResults  from  the  survey  regarding  briefing  effectiveness and  MVI  compliance  as  well  as  routinely  collected  data regarding injuries and training delays of the participants are\\n\\n--- Page 4 ---\\nTABLE III. Survey, Injury, and Training Results\\nThe bold values represent statistical significance (\\ud835\\udefc \\u2264 0.05).\\nsummarized in Table III. There were no losses or exclusions of routinely collected and linked data.\\nIn regard to the briefing, there were no significant differences between cohorts in proportion of trainees reporting that they found the brief to be effective in explaining why the MVI was prescribed. However, there was a significantly larger proportion of those within the cohort that received the in-person brief  who  stated  they  felt  confident  in  their  understanding of  why  they  were  prescribed  the  MVI  (100%  vs.  90.41%, P = .007).\\nIn  regard  to  compliance, compared  to  the  video-only cohort, a significantly higher proportion within the in-person cohort, a significantly higher proportion within the in-person cohort  reported  taking  the  MVI  on  most  days  (or  more) (63.01% vs.  37.84%, P = .0023),  and  a  significantly  lower proportion reported never taking the MVI (8.22% vs. 20.27%, P = .037).\\nIn  regard  to  injury,  a  significantly  smaller  proportion  of the  in-person  cohort  suffered  MSKI  (17.72%  vs.  31.25%, P = .047) and BSI (5.06% vs.  15%, P = .037) compared to the video-only cohort.\\nIn regard to training delays, there were no significant differences of proportion of trainees who were sent to medical hold or recycled in training between cohorts.\\nDISCUSSION\\nFrom  the  results  of  this  study,  we  infer  that  incorporating an in-person brief from SMEs improved compliance with the MVI which in turn significantly reduced injuries. The relative and absolute risk reductions for diagnosis with all MSKI were 43% and 13.5%,  respectively.  This  absolute  risk  reduction corresponds to a number needed to in-person brief (NNIPB) of 7.4 to avoid one MSKI. Said another way, with \\u223c 40 female trainees in a briefing,  each in-person brief delivered would be expected to prevent 5.4 MSKI compared to the video-only brief. The relative and absolute risk reductions for diagnosis with BSI were 66% and 10%, respectively; this corresponds to  a  NNIPB  of  10.  Said  another  way,  each  in-person  brief (of  40  female  trainees)  would  be  expected  to  prevent  four BSIs.  Based  on  current  literature  on  nutritional  deficiency, dietary supplementation, and BSI risk, the iron 22,33 and vitamin D/calcium 28 content of the MVI is suspected to have been most beneficial to BSI reduction in this study. Though less is known regarding the association with injury and efficacy for risk reduction of other vitamins and minerals in the MVI, they may also have supported healthy tissue adaptations to training stress.\\nAlthough neither this prospective study nor the retrospective  study  by  Barnes  et al.  detected  significant  differences in training disruption, we showed a significant difference in BSI,  whereas  Barnes  et al.  did  not. 35 This  is  likely  due  to this study's randomized nature as opposed to using a historical,  season-matched comparison group as the control.  Our design controlled for temporal fluctuations in diagnostic patterns,  access  to  care,  care-seeking  behaviors,  and  training activities and policies, which may have skewed the findings of the prior study. The lack of significant difference in attrition despite differences in BSI, as was also the finding in a recent randomized controlled trial by Kasper et al., 24 is a testament to the early identification and efficient rehabilitation of MSKI provided by the BMT sports medicine team, which was implemented specifically to mitigate the operational impact of injury at BMT. 25\\nThis study was limited in several ways: (1) it used block rather than individual randomization, (2) all trainees received the MVI (because of the potential benefits of the MVI), (3) it did not collect data regarding existing nutritional deficiencies, and (4) it was only conducted on a single BMT iteration so it cannot be known how the difference in season may affect the outcome. Despite these limitations, it adds to the body of knowledge regarding the benefits of this approach in female military trainees. Besides the presence and engagement of the SMEs at the briefing,  to  the  authors'  knowledge,  no  other differences in training or healthcare occurred between these two groups to explain the decrease in BSI. Flights within a squadron undergo nearly identical training, tissue loads, and access to medical care (the same embedded athletic trainers and sports medicine physicians), so it is unlikely that being in  different  flights  alone  would  account  for  the  differences in injury diagnoses. A 2022 study of the implementation of mass running gait training at BMT found that trainees who experienced a face-to-face encounter with medical personnel, who introduced themselves as available to help with issues related  to  BMT  completion,  reduced  hesitancy  to  be  seen, and  subsequently  increased  BSI  diagnoses. 38 With  a  similar interaction between trainees and embedded medical staff in  our  study  potentially  also  increasing  trainee  willingness to  report  symptoms,  resultant  injury  diagnoses  could  have been promoted among the in-person MVI-briefing cohort, 38 but  there  were  still  significantly  fewer  injury  diagnoses  in this cohort. Overweight and obesity is common in the U.S. Military (following training), and programs are in place throughout the DoD to address this. 39 However, it is important to remember the nutritionally related health and performance issues related to the underconsumption of nutrients within military training situations to fuel necessary performance and required physical adaptations 17 ; nutritional programs must be specific to the particular setting or goal (training vs. readiness maintenance). Interventions  aimed  at  overcoming  deficiencies  relative  to training and providing the timely delivery of relevant health and  performance  nutrition  education  and  interventions  are vital in improving success rates at BMT. Nutritional supplementation  in  military  training  should  be  further  studied  to verify its efficacy in injury reduction in at-risk populations and improve formulations specific to the needs of the population.
At  the  time  of  this  study, the  standard  was  to  brief trainees  on  the  MVI  via  video,  which  avoided  repetitively burdening  the  clinical  staff  with  being  present  for  multiple  briefings  each  week  at  various  times.  Although  simplification  and  automation  are  often  valuable  for  repetitive processes,  this study shows that an automated (video-only) MVI  briefing  at  BMT  was  associated  with  worse  compliance  and  injury  rates  than  an  in-person  briefing.  In-person medical  intervention  education  by  interested  SMEs,  albeit more burdensome, has demonstrable benefits on the learner's confidence in their understanding and compliance. The cost and  benefits  of  educational  modalities  regarding  individual or  population  health  measures  should  be  carefully  considered,  and whenever feasible and cost effective,  face-to-face educational  approaches  should  be  undertaken. Since  this study, embedded RDs have regularly delivered the BMT MVI briefings.

Korey B. Kasper, MD, CAQSM *; Meredith Cockerell, MS,  ATC†; Clarissa Escamilla, MS, RDN, LD‡;

Richard Gonzalez, MDS, RDN, LD‡

## ABSTRACT

## Introduction:
10→
Department of the Air Force basic military training (BMT) is the 7.5-week initial entry training for all enlisting U.S. Air Force and Space Force recruits. Overuse musculoskeletal injuries (MSKI) during training threaten success in BMT, and trainees with nutritional deficiencies are at higher risk. Several efforts are made at BMT to mitigate these issues to help trainees graduate on time, such as the distribution of multivitamins (MVI) to female recruits. However, trainee compliance with the prescribed MVI has been reported to be low, calling into question the effectiveness of this intervention. This study evaluated the effect of briefing modality offered to these trainees at the time of distribution on educational effectiveness, MVI compliance, and injury rates.

## Materials and Methods:

This was a randomized controlled cohort study of BMT female trainees. Subjects included all female trainees of a single iteration of BMT concurrently completing training within the same squadron. At the outset of training, cohorts were randomly educated in one of two ways regarding the provided MVI. The control cohort ( n = 80) was presented with the standard educational video created by BMT-registered dietitians, while the test cohort ( n = 79) was presented the video and then also briefed in-person by a group of subject matter experts. At the end of BMT, the trainees completed a questionnaire regarding their knowledge, confidence, and compliance with the MVI. findings.location: Table III, survey rows (brief effectiveness and MVI compliance)
findings.quote: Furthermore, all trainees completed questionnaires regarding their perceptions regarding the usefulness and effectiveness of their MVI briefing and were asked to quantify their MVI compliance.

consequence.explanation: Chi-squared p-values in Table III match the implied survey ns of 73–74, so the significance claims survive; the printed column ns of 80 and 79 are not the analysis denominators.

findings.notes: Tool grim_sweep returned empty joint n-set for the five video-only survey percentages over the stated n_max=80 (verdict impossible). Downgraded to suspicious: the percentages are uniquely recovered at n=73 (briefing items) and n=74 (compliance items), and the in-person survey items share a unique n=73 rather than 79. Recalculated chi-squared p-values from those reconstructed 2×2 tables match the printed p-values, so the authors analysed the smaller denominators. The 6–7 person gap exceeds the three-patient-or-5%-of-n missingness bound (Rule 15), and Methods states all trainees completed questionnaires, which is an explicit completeness claim for these rows. Innocent reading is item-level nonresponse under an enrollment header. GRIM-family impossible verdicts await the R scrutiny cross-check (editorial stage).
findings.reproduction_problem: THE COMMAND DISAGREES WITH THE FINDING: it reports `impossible` where the finding claims `suspicious`. The command ran perfectly well -- that is the point. Re-read the finding before the paper.

severity_source.note: The tool returned `impossible`; this finding records `suspicious`. A reason is stated in the finding.

findings.notes: Nine two-decimal survey percentages fail GRIM at the column header ns (80 and 79); 100% in-person confidence is the only survey cell that passes at n=79. check_table on Table III ran 22 grim_percentage checks: 10 impossible, 9 consistent, 3 indeterminate (0-dp cells with no discriminating power). The 10 impossibles are these survey cells plus video-only Medical hold 1.27%.
